learningObjectives.title: Reactivity 3.1 HL: pH, Ka/Kb and buffers

questions.q: pH is defined by the expression:
questions.explain: pH is the negative logarithm (base 10) of the hydrogen-ion concentration.

questions.q: A solution has [H+] = 1 x 10^-3 mol/dm3. Its pH is:
A strong acid of concentration 0.010 mol/dm3 (fully dissociated) has a pH of:
The ionic product of water, Kw, at 25 degrees C is:
questions.explain: Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14 mol2 dm^-6 at 25 degrees C.

questions.q: A solution has [OH-] = 1 x 10^-2 mol/dm3. Its pH is:
A larger value of Ka indicates that an acid is:
questions.explain: A larger acid dissociation constant means greater dissociation and a stronger acid.

questions.q: The relationship between Ka and pKa is:
questions.explain: A smaller pKa corresponds to a larger Ka and a stronger acid.

questions.q: Acid X has pKa 3.2 and acid Y has pKa 4.8. Which is the stronger acid?
questions.explain: The lower pKa (X) corresponds to the larger Ka and the stronger acid.

questions.q: A buffer solution is one that:
options: Resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
questions.explain: Buffers minimise pH change through an equilibrium between conjugate species.

questions.q: An acidic buffer is typically made from:
options: A weak acid and its conjugate base (salt)
A strong acid and a strong base
questions.explain: For example, ethanoic acid with sodium ethanoate forms an acidic buffer.

questions.q: A buffer works because it contains reservoirs that can:
options: Neutralise added acid and added base
questions.explain: The weak acid neutralises added base and the conjugate base neutralises added acid.

questions.q: When [acid] = [conjugate base] in a buffer, the pH equals:
questions.explain: From the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship, pH = pKa when the ratio is 1.

questions.q: The pH of a 0.10 mol/dm3 solution of a strong base NaOH is:
A weak acid at the same concentration as a strong acid has a higher pH because it has:
options: More hydroxide ions than the strong acid
questions.explain: Partial dissociation gives fewer H+ ions, so a higher pH.

questions.q: The pH at the equivalence point of a strong acid-strong base titration is approximately:
questions.explain: The salt formed is neutral, giving pH 7 at equivalence for a strong acid-strong base.

questions.q: The equivalence point of a weak acid titrated with a strong base is:
questions.explain: The salt of a weak acid and strong base is basic, so the equivalence pH is above 7.

questions.q: If the pH of a solution decreases by 2 units, the hydrogen-ion concentration:
questions.explain: A decrease of 2 pH units means [H+] rises by 10^2 = 100 times.

questions.q: For a conjugate acid-base pair at 25 degrees C, pKa + pKb equals:
questions.explain: Because Ka x Kb = Kw, pKa + pKb = 14 at 25 degrees C.

questions.q: A blood buffer keeps pH near 7.4 using the equilibrium of carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate. Adding a small amount of acid is neutralised by:
questions.explain: The conjugate base (HCO3-) reacts with added H+ to limit the pH change.
